sn22.62:1.2: The three “scopes” or “ranges” (_patha_) are the past, present, and future, each of which is indicated by the appropriate grammatical tense. | _Nirutti_ means the “clear expression” or “definition” of a word. In the pre-Buddhist literature, that which is “undefined” is the mystical truth to be muttered under the breath, whereas that which is “defined” is clearly expressed in language. A list of such definitions is a _nirukti_, a glossary or dictionary. See [dn15:32.11](), [mn139:13.55](), and [an5.169:3.6]().
sn22.62:1.5: The purpose of this argument is to rebut the idea that “being” or “existence” is eternal, and change an illusion. The Buddha points out that ordinary usage describes things that exist as impermanent, and thus the eternalist thesis contradicts the commonly-agreed truth. This passage is cited in [kv1.7]() against the Sarvāstivādin thesis that all phenomena of past, present, and future, exist (also discussed at [kv1.6]() and [kv1.8]()).
sn22.62:13.2: This pair is also mentioned in the same way regarding different teachings at [mn117:38.1]() and especially [an4.30:8.2](), which was probably the original context, and which identifies them as “wanderers”. Nothing is known of them apart from these passages. | Ukkalā lay on the Bay of Bengal in the region today called Odisha. It was the origin of the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika who offered the first meal to the Buddha ([pli-tv-kd1:4.2.1](), [an1.248:1.1]()).
